source.title: Which transformer architecture fits my data? A vocabulary bottleneck in self-attention
source.authors: Noam Wies; Yoav Levine; Daniel Jannai; A. Shashua

record.tranche_reason: The study tests how architecture choices affect held-out language-model loss using controlled training comparisons, but does not apply the original scaling-law fitting method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports architecture and held-out-loss experiments relevant to V4. It does not fit power laws in parameters, tokens, or compute; test extrapolation from smaller runs; find a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation; test other modalities experimentally; or evaluate downstream-task predictability. Cited results from other work and the paper's theoretical separation-rank arguments are not recorded as empirical rows.
record.test_reason: The paper's own controlled pretraining runs compare held-out LM loss across architectures of similar parameter count. It varies depth (24 vs 48; 12/18/24), width, input embedding rank, positional rank and attention-dimension ratio, which bears directly on V4. It fits no power laws, tests no extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, other modalities or downstream tasks.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add the authors' central claim: cross-domain differences in optimal depth-to-width ratio come from vocabulary size or embedding rank (an expressivity bottleneck), not from data modality. Also add their estimates of 25–50% size redundancy in ALBERT and T5.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies embedding rank and architecture configurations and compares held-out language-model loss; it does not fit scaling laws or extrapolate loss from smaller runs.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed depth-to-width tradeoff changes with vocabulary size and embedding rank. Loss also changes with the internal attention-to-width ratio.
record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 139, 2021
record.problems: The paper reports many plotted comparisons without exact individual loss values in the text. The experiments use its own decoder-only language models and training setup; several architecture-wide claims are also supported by theory rather than experimental tests across diverse model families.
record.rows_left_out: No additional empirical architecture/loss results relevant to V4 were left out. Cited external results and theoretical arguments were excluded because they are not outcomes from the study's own experiments.

untested.parts: No power-law fits in parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
Model sizes are only 5M–110M, there is one training recipe (1M steps, 128-token context), and feed-forward ratio is not varied.
Only text LMs are trained; claims about image and protein models are inferred, not tested.
No fitting choices or exponents are examined.

missing.what: Depth-variation result: the loss spread across depths 12/18/24 at each attention ratio is much smaller than the spread between ratios, which bears on V4 support for depth.
Rank-1 positional embedding reaches the loss of a vocabulary-rank 64–128 model. Embedding ranks above width (880, 1080) were also trained in the rank sweep.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'challenges' label is replaced with limits_scope. The effects are absolute loss changes of a few percent, the same order as the original's shape effects, and V4 is qualified rather than refuted: shape matters when bottlenecks exist. The row states R3, R4, R5 and R6 had been judged against the paper's depth-advantage hypothesis rather than V4; they are fixed above.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss across parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as a function of compute.
The study varies embedding rank, depth, width, and internal attention dimension, but does not systematically vary every architecture detail or establish a general result across all model families.
The experiments are language-model experiments; the paper does not test the claimed power-law form in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream-task performance and its predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and bending away from a single power law.

rows.subject: depth-12 decoder-only language models (rank sweep aggregate)
rows.size_stated: 50M to 75M parameters for full-rank baselines; low-rank models used width 680
rows.operation_detail: Trained models while varying input embedding rank and, for comparison, width.

conditions.value: varied from 16 to full rank dx=680

rows.value: Loss increased much more rapidly when input embedding rank was reduced than when network size was reduced by decreasing width.
rows.uncertainty: Reported test loss stable up to 10^-3; seven architectures were rerun five times each.
rows.note: The text describes the rank-sweep outcome qualitatively; individual plotted loss values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: State is correct for V4. Fig. 2 shows loss rising from about 2.385 to 2.44 as rank falls from 680 to 16 at fixed width. That is a modest absolute change, but it equals about 25% of parameters, so the architecture detail matters more than V4 implies.

rows.subject: depth-12 decoder-only language model
rows.operation_detail: Trained a width-680 model with input embedding rank 16 and compared its loss with a smaller full-rank network.
rows.baseline: A full-rank network with 25% fewer parameters
rows.value: The approximately 70-million-parameter low-rank network was comparable in performance to the full-rank network that was 25% smaller.
rows.note: The comparison shows a substantial loss cost from this architecture choice; no exact loss values are stated in the text.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.1, paragraph following the weight-tying control: approximately 70M parameters, r/dx=16/680, comparable performance to a full-rank network 25% smaller.

rows.subject: decoder-only language models, L=24 versus L=48
rows.operation_detail: Compared shallow and deep architectures across model sizes using vocabulary size 257.
rows.value: L=48 models began outperforming the shallow models sooner; the plotted shallow width at the transition was 224.
rows.note: The paper describes the depth advantage and gives the transition width in the figure caption.
rows.check: State was 'observed' for the depth advantage, but it should be judged against V4 (shape matters little). At V=257 the 48-layer model beats the 24-layer model at similar size, so depth/width matters here and V4 holds only partially.

rows.subject: decoder-only language models, L=24 versus L=48
rows.operation_detail: Compared shallow and deep architectures across model sizes using vocabulary size 500.
rows.value: L=48 models began outperforming the shallow models sooner; the plotted shallow width at the transition was 408.
rows.note: The paper reports that the smaller vocabulary produces an earlier depth-efficiency transition than the larger-vocabulary case.
rows.check: Same direction problem as R3. At V=500 depth beats width at fixed size, so V4 holds only partially.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.2.1; Figure 1(b); Section 5.2.2 continuation gives shallow transition width approximately 408.

rows.subject: decoder-only language models, L=24 versus L=48
rows.operation_detail: Compared shallow and deep architectures across model sizes using vocabulary size 2000.
rows.value: The advantage of deeper models disappears when the vocabulary is larger than the network width; the plotted shallow width was 408.
rows.note: The text says the deeper-network advantage disappears in this setting.
rows.check: State was 'absent' for the depth advantage. Relative to V4 it should be 'observed': with no vocabulary bottleneck (V=2000), shallow and deep networks of similar size perform comparably.

source_check.locator_found: Figure 1(c) and caption; Section 4.2.2 describes comparable performance before the embedding-rank bottleneck.

rows.subject: decoder-only language models, L=24 versus L=48
rows.operation_detail: Compared shallow and deep architectures while restricting the input embedding rank.
rows.value: The deeper network surpassed the shallower one when the latter's width reached the embedding rank; the reported transition width was 504.
rows.note: This comparison holds vocabulary size fixed and varies embedding rank.
rows.check: Same direction problem as R3. With embedding rank restricted to 500, depth gains an advantage once shallow width reaches 504, so shape matters in this setting.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.2.2 and Figure 3: vocabulary 2000, rank 500, depths 24 and 48, shallow transition width 504.

rows.subject: decoder-only language models, L=24 versus L=48
rows.operation_detail: Compared depth-efficiency transitions with vocabulary sizes 2000 and 50257.
rows.measure: held-out test loss and depth-efficiency transition
rows.value: The much larger GPT-2 vocabulary had a very similar depth-efficiency point; the shallow width at that point was also described as very similar.
rows.uncertainty: Table 4 reports standard deviations for selected runs; the comparison's exact uncertainty is not stated.
rows.note: The text states that the vocabulary size is about 25 times larger and that the transition points are similar.
rows.check: This row compares vocabulary sizes rather than shapes directly. The depth-efficiency point is at shallow width ~704 for both V=2000 and V=50257, consistent with depth and width being comparable below that point. Its bearing on V4 is indirect.

source_check.correct: The depth-efficiency transition occurs at shallow width approximately 704 for both vocabularies, although its parameter count differs because of embedding size. This establishes insensitivity of the transition width to vocabulary size above network width; it does not establish nearly invariant loss under depth/width changes. For that V4 interpretation, use cannot_determine.
source_check.locator_found: Appendix C.2, Figure 5 and adjoining paragraphs.
source_check.problem: The observed state treats vocabulary-insensitive transition width as evidence of shape-insensitive loss.

rows.subject: decoder-only language models with varied internal attention dimension
rows.operation_detail: Varied the ratio of internal attention representation to network width, choosing the best depth from 12, 18, and 24 for each ratio and size.
rows.value: Performance degraded as the bottleneck ratio increased; the text reports monotone degradation across ratios but gives no separate numerical loss for ratio 2.
rows.note: The paper states the monotone trend, but not the individual loss difference for this ratio.
rows.check: No numeric value is stated; it rests only on the stated monotone degradation. Could be read from Fig. 4.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.3, Figure 4; Appendix C.3: ratios 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16, monotonically worsening performance, best depth selected from 12, 18 and 24.

rows.subject: decoder-only language models with varied internal attention dimension
rows.operation_detail: Varied the ratio of internal attention representation to network width, choosing the best depth from 12, 18, and 24 for each ratio and size.
rows.value: A network with this ratio achieved performance that a baseline network could reach with approximately 75% of its parameters.
rows.note: The text connects this ratio to the second-largest T5 model and reports the approximate parameter redundancy.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.3, paragraph discussing the T5-3B configuration: ratio 4 matches a baseline with approximately 75% of the parameters.

rows.operation_detail: Varied the ratio of internal attention representation to network width, choosing the best depth from 12, 18, and 24 for each ratio and size.
rows.value: Performance degraded as the bottleneck ratio increased; the text reports monotone degradation across ratios but gives no separate numerical loss for ratio 8.
rows.note: The paper states the monotone trend, but not the individual loss difference for this ratio.

rows.subject: decoder-only language models with varied internal attention dimension
rows.operation_detail: Varied the ratio of internal attention representation to network width, choosing the best depth from 12, 18, and 24 for each ratio and size.
rows.value: A baseline network with approximately 55% of the parameters could achieve the performance of a network with this ratio.
rows.note: The text estimates approximately 45% parameter redundancy for the largest T5 model configuration.

rows.subject: depth-12 decoder-only language models
rows.operation_detail: Varied positional embedding rank and compared it with models using reduced vocabulary rank.
rows.value: Positional rank 16 performed on par with full positional embedding, within 2 standard deviations.
rows.note: The paper describes the effect of this positional-rank reduction as negligible relative to the vocabulary-rank effect.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix C.4, Figure 7 and adjoining paragraphs: depth 12, width 512, vocabulary 2000, sequence length 512, positional rank 16 on par with full rank within two standard deviations.

relationships.condition: No vocabulary or embedding-rank bottleneck (vocabulary at or above width); depth choice within a fixed attention ratio; positional embedding rank ≥16
relationships.reason: Depth 24 vs 48 performs comparably at similar size when V=2000 or 50257 is not a bottleneck (R5, R7). Positional rank 16 is on par with full rank (R12). Fig. 6 shows small depth variation (12/18/24), per the text.
relationships.display_finding: Depths 24 and 48 performed comparably in the tested comparison, positional rank 16 matched full rank, and depths 12, 18 and 24 varied little within a fixed attention ratio.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: No vocabulary or embedding-rank bottleneck (vocabulary at or above width); depth choice within a fixed attention ratio; positional embedding rank ≥16
source_check.reason: Retain supports with a narrower condition: the Figure 1(c) depth comparison (R5), tested positional ranks down to 16 (R12), and relatively small within-ratio depth variation in Figure 6. R7 establishes vocabulary-insensitive transition width, not depth/width loss invariance; absence of a vocabulary bottleneck alone is insufficient, since Figure 5 still reports depth-efficiency transitions.

relationships.condition: Input vocabulary size or embedding rank below network width
relationships.reason: Reducing embedding rank costs loss equal to ~25% of parameters (R1, R2). When vocab or rank is below width, deeper models outperform shallower ones of equal size (R3, R4, R6), so the depth/width split matters there.
relationships.display_finding: Reducing embedding rank incurred a loss penalty equivalent to losing about 25% of parameters, and deeper models outperformed equally sized shallow models when vocabulary size or rank fell below width.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Input vocabulary size or embedding rank below network width
source_check.reason: R1–R2 show a substantial parameter-efficiency cost from low embedding rank; R3–R4 and R6 show depth preferences changing with vocabulary or embedding rank. These results qualify architectural insensitivity.

relationships.condition: Internal attention dimension H·da exceeding width dx (ratios 2–16)
relationships.reason: Loss degrades monotonically with the ratio. Ratio 4 matches a baseline with ~75% of the parameters and ratio 16 one with ~55% (R8–R11), so heads/attention-dimension choices are not loss-neutral.
relationships.display_finding: Loss worsened monotonically as attention dimension exceeded width; ratios of 4 and 16 matched baselines with only about 75% and 55% as many parameters, respectively.

relation.reason: The study reports its own parameter-matched architecture comparisons bearing on V4.

tranche.reason: Controlled architecture and embedding-rank sweeps measure held-out language-model loss and directly test V4 through a different experimental design.

source_check.notes: The T5 and ALBERT redundancy estimates are projections from smaller controlled models, not direct retraining results for those published checkpoints. Statements were checked only for claims attributable to this study; the other studies' numbers were outside this check.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Depth comparisons without a vocabulary or embedding-rank bottleneck, and positional embedding rank 16
reader_labels.reason: The depth advantage disappears with vocabulary size 2000 when it is not a bottleneck, the GPT-2 vocabulary gives a similar transition point, and positional rank 16 is on par with full rank (R5, R7, R12).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Reduced input embedding rank or internal attention dimension exceeding network width
reader_labels.reason: Loss worsens with reduced embedding rank, and excess internal attention dimensions cause reported parameter redundancy, including approximately 25% for ratio 4 and approximately 45% for ratio 16 (R1, R2, R9, R11).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Depth/width comparisons when vocabulary size or embedding rank is below the shallow model's width
reader_labels.reason: Deeper models outperform shallower ones in these tested bottleneck settings, but not in the unbottlenecked vocabulary-size-2000 setting (R3, R4, R5, R6).
